examples.en: An angry customer made a scene in the shop.

examples.ko: 제발 오늘 회의에서 깽판 놓지 마세요.
examples.en: Please don't wreck the meeting today.

examples.ko: 네가 깽판 쳐서 계획이 다 엉망이 됐어요.
examples.en: You messed it up, and now the whole plan is a wreck.

examples.ko: 일부러 깽판 놓으려고 온 사람 같아요.
examples.en: He seems like someone who came on purpose to cause trouble.

examples.ko: 동생이 방에서 깽판을 친 걸 엄마가 보셨어요.
examples.en: Mom saw that my little brother had trashed the room.
A ruckus broke out at the party and everyone was shocked.

explain: '깽판을 치다', '깽판을 놓다'처럼 거의 이 형태로 써요. 일이 잘 안 되게 망치거나 소란을 피울 때 쓰는 구어체라서 친구나 가족 사이에서 자연스럽고, 격식 있는 자리에서는 '망치다'나 '소란을 피우다'를 써요.
explain_en: It is used almost only in the forms '깽판을 치다' and '깽판을 놓다'. It is colloquial for ruining something or causing a ruckus, so it fits among friends and family. In formal settings people say '망치다' or '소란을 피우다'.

examples.en: I put out the candle by mistake.
Be careful not to let the campfire go out.
The wind is strong, so I keep letting the match go out.

examples.ko: 난로 불씨를 꺼뜨리면 다시 피우기 힘들어요.
examples.en: If you let the stove embers die, it's hard to light them again.

examples.ko: 아기가 후 불어서 생일 초를 다 꺼뜨렸어요.
examples.en: The baby blew and put out all the birthday candles.
I stalled the engine and the car stopped suddenly.

explain: '끄다'는 일부러 끌 때 쓰고, '꺼뜨리다'는 실수나 부주의로 불이 꺼지게 했을 때 많이 써요. '꺼트리다'로도 써요. 불, 촛불, 불씨뿐 아니라 운전할 때 '시동을 꺼뜨리다'처럼도 말해요.
explain_en: '끄다' is for turning something off on purpose, while '꺼뜨리다' often suggests you let a fire go out by mistake or carelessness. You can also say '꺼트리다'. It is used for fires, candles and embers, and also in driving, as in '시동을 꺼뜨리다' (to stall the engine).

examples.en: Somehow what that person said bothers me.

examples.ko: 계약서에 서명하는 게 아직 꺼림해서 한 번 더 읽어 봤어요.
examples.en: I still felt uneasy about signing the contract, so I read it once more.

examples.ko: 중고 물건을 사는 게 좀 꺼림하지 않아요?
examples.en: Doesn't buying secondhand things bother you a bit?

examples.ko: 마음이 꺼림해서 그냥 전화를 걸어 봤어요.
examples.en: I felt uneasy, so I just gave a call.

examples.ko: 그 일에는 어딘가 꺼림한 구석이 있어요.
examples.en: There is something off about that matter.
I left the house feeling uneasy.

explain: '꺼림칙하다'와 거의 같은 말인데, 마음에 걸려서 개운하지 않은 느낌이에요. 보통 '마음이 꺼림하다', '꺼림한 기분'처럼 마음 상태와 함께 써요.
explain_en: It is nearly the same as '꺼림칙하다': a nagging feeling that something is not quite right. It usually goes with the mind or mood, as in '마음이 꺼림하다' or '꺼림한 기분'.

examples.en: Don't I look like a real goof?
My little brother sometimes acts like a goofball, and it's funny.
Don't tease me by calling me a goof.

examples.ko: 그 아이는 꺼벙이 같아도 마음은 착해요.
examples.en: That kid may seem goofy, but he has a kind heart.

examples.ko: 우산을 또 놓고 왔어요? 완전 꺼벙이네요.
examples.en: You left your umbrella behind again? What a goof.
My friend calls me a goof.

explain: 조금 어리숙하고 덜렁대는 사람을 놀리듯 부르는 말이에요. 심한 욕이라기보다 친한 사이에서 가볍게 쓰는 경우가 많아서, 윗사람이나 처음 만난 사람에게는 쓰지 않는 게 좋아요.
explain_en: It is a teasing word for someone a bit slow-witted or absent-minded. It is often used lightly between close friends rather than as a harsh insult, but avoid it with elders or people you've just met.

examples.en: The child fell and wailed.
Everyone sobbed loudly at the end of the movie.

examples.ko: 친구가 이별 얘기를 하며 꺼이꺼이 울더라고요.
examples.en: My friend bawled while talking about the breakup.

examples.ko: 그는 합격 소식에 꺼이꺼이 소리 내어 울었어요.
examples.en: He cried out loud, sobbing, at the news that he passed.
I could hear loud sobbing from the next room.

examples.ko: 꺼이꺼이 울고 나니까 마음이 좀 가벼워졌어요.
examples.en: After sobbing my heart out, I felt a bit lighter.

explain: 거의 '울다'와 함께 쓰고, 목이 메어 숨을 끊어 가며 크게 우는 소리를 나타내요. '엉엉'은 소리 내어 크게 우는 모양이고, '꺼이꺼이'는 목이 메어 울음이 끊기는 느낌이 더 강해요.
explain_en: It is used almost only with '울다' and describes crying hard with a choked voice, breaking for breath. '엉엉' is loud crying in general, while '꺼이꺼이' stresses the choked, broken sound.

examples.en: My hands are so rough.
I haven't slept for days, so my skin is rough and dull.
I wiped my face with a scratchy towel.
I didn't shave, so my chin got stubbly.
In winter my lips get rough, so I put on balm.
The surface of this paper is rough.

explain: '꺼칠하다'를 반복해서 거칠고 마른 느낌을 더 강조한 말이에요. 피부, 입술, 머리카락, 수염처럼 만졌을 때 매끄럽지 않은 것에 많이 써요. 반대로 매끄럽고 부드러우면 '부드럽다'라고 해요.
explain_en: It repeats '꺼칠하다' to stress a rough, dry feel. It is common for skin, lips, hair and stubble, things that feel not smooth to the touch. The opposite is '부드럽다' (soft, smooth).

examples.en: I woke up and my face looks haggard.
My hair was rough, so I bought a treatment.
His face has become quite haggard in a few days.
I feel bad touching the baby with my rough hands.
I was tired and went to work looking worn out.
I washed a puppy with coarse fur.

explain: '거칠다'와 비슷하지만, 얼굴이나 피부가 마르고 윤기가 없어서 피곤해 보인다는 느낌이 자주 들어가요. '얼굴이 꺼칠해지다'는 건강이 안 좋아 보일 때 쓰는 말이에요.
explain_en: It is similar to '거칠다' (rough), but often carries a sense of dry, dull skin that makes someone look tired. '얼굴이 꺼칠해지다' is what you say when someone looks unwell.

examples.ko: 양파 꺼풀을 한 겹 벗겨 내세요.
examples.en: Peel off one layer of the onion.
My skin got sunburned and a layer peeled off.

examples.ko: 양파 겉의 마른 꺼풀은 먹지 않아요.
examples.en: I don't eat the dry outer layer of an onion.
An onion has many layers.

examples.ko: 껍질을 벗기니 속에 얇은 꺼풀이 또 있어요.
examples.en: After peeling it, there is another thin layer inside.
Please peel the garlic and mince it.

explain: '껍질'이 겉을 싼 것 전체라면, '꺼풀'은 여러 겹으로 된 것의 한 겹을 말할 때 잘 어울려요. 혼자 쓰는 것보다 '눈꺼풀', '쌍꺼풀'처럼 합쳐진 말로 더 자주 만나요.
explain_en: While '껍질' is the whole outer covering, '꺼풀' fits when talking about one layer of something made of several layers. You meet it more often in compounds like '눈꺼풀' (eyelid) and '쌍꺼풀' (double eyelid).

examples.en: My little brother is tall, so his nickname is Beanpole.
That tall guy over there is my uncle.

examples.ko: 꺽다리와 키 작은 친구가 늘 같이 다녀요.
examples.en: The tall guy and his short friend always go around together.
There are a lot of tall guys on the basketball team.
That tall guy bumped his head on the door frame.
When I was little, I got teased as a beanpole.

explain: 키가 큰 사람, 특히 키가 크고 좀 마른 사람을 장난스럽게 부를 때 써요. '키다리'도 비슷한 말이고, 반대로 키가 작은 사람은 '땅딸보'라고 놀리듯 부르기도 해요.
explain_en: It playfully refers to a tall person, especially a tall and rather thin one. '키다리' is a similar word, and the opposite, teasingly, is '땅딸보' for a short person.

examples.en: Grandfather heard the joke and laughed heartily.

examples.ko: 아버님은 속이 시원하신 듯이 껄껄 웃으셨어요.
examples.en: Father laughed heartily as if he felt relieved.

examples.ko: 박사님은 제자의 재치 있는 농담에 껄껄 웃으셨어요.
examples.en: The professor roared with laughter at his student's witty joke.

examples.ko: 사장님은 제 실수를 보고도 껄껄 웃고 넘어가셨어요.
examples.en: The boss saw my mistake and just laughed it off.
My uncle always talks with a hearty laugh.

examples.ko: 어르신들이 껄껄 웃으며 옛날이야기를 해 주셨어요.
examples.en: The elders told us old stories with hearty laughter.

explain: '껄껄 웃다'처럼 쓰고, 어른이 기분 좋게 크게 웃는 호탕한 웃음이 떠오르는 말이에요. 아이들이나 젊은 사람이 높고 경쾌하게 웃을 때는 '깔깔'을 많이 써요.
explain_en: Used as '껄껄 웃다', it evokes a hearty, good-natured laugh, often of an older person. A high, light laugh of children or young people is usually '깔깔'.

examples.en: Grandfather is laughing heartily watching TV.
The guests roared with laughter at a single joke.
The men sit around talking and laughing loudly.
Father was in a good mood and laughing all day.

examples.ko: 너무 껄껄거리지 말고 조용히 해 주세요.
examples.en: Please don't guffaw so much and keep it down.
The sound of loud laughter reaches the hallway.

explain: '껄껄 웃다'를 한 동사로 말한 거예요. '-거리다'는 같은 동작이 이어진다는 느낌이 있어서 계속 크게 웃는 모습에 어울려요. 윗사람이 웃을 때는 '껄껄거리셨어요'처럼 높여요.
explain_en: It is '껄껄 웃다' packed into one verb. '-거리다' gives a feel of continued action, so it suits ongoing loud laughter. For someone senior, use the honorific form, like '껄껄거리셨어요'.

examples.en: My friends are laughing loudly watching a cartoon.
Every time we meet, he greets me with a hearty laugh.
The boys were guffawing in the back.
Stop guffawing and tell me why.
Grandfather roared with laughter at his grandchild's antics.
I woke up to my coworkers' loud laughter.

explain: '껄껄거리다'와 같은 뜻으로 바꿔 쓸 수 있어요. 둘 다 '껄껄 웃다'를 한 동사로 만든 말이고, 크게 웃는 소리가 계속 들릴 때 써요. 윗사람이 웃으면 '껄껄대셨어요'처럼 높여요.
explain_en: It can replace '껄껄거리다' with the same meaning. Both turn '껄껄 웃다' into one verb for loud laughter that keeps going. For someone senior, use the honorific, like '껄껄대셨어요'.

examples.en: My throat felt scratchy, so I drank some water.
For some reason things are awkward between that person and me.
Let's talk about the awkward stuff later.
I have a cold and my throat is scratchy.
Since our fight, it's awkward to meet my friend.

examples.ko: 이 천은 만지면 껄끄러운 느낌이 나요.
examples.en: This fabric feels scratchy to the touch.

explain: 촉감이 거칠다는 뜻도 있지만, 사람 사이가 어색하고 불편할 때도 많이 써요. '불편하다'보다 은근히 어색하고 마주하기 부담스러운 느낌이에요. 'ㅂ' 불규칙이라서 '껄끄러워요', '껄끄러운'으로 바뀌어요.
explain_en: It can describe a rough, scratchy feel, and it is also often used when a relationship is awkward. Compared with '불편하다', it suggests a subtle awkwardness that makes facing someone burdensome. It is a ㅂ-irregular adjective, so it becomes '껄끄러워요' and '껄끄러운'.

examples.en: I'm sleepy and keep blinking slowly.
The child looked at me, blinking.
The fluorescent light is flickering and my eyes hurt.
The cow is blinking its big eyes.
He just blinked, as if he didn't understand.
The light flickered and then went out.

explain: '깜박거리다'의 큰말이라서 눈이나 불빛이 크고 느릿하게 깜빡이는 느낌이에요. 눈을 감았다 뜨는 모습뿐 아니라 불빛이 꺼질 듯 말 듯할 때도 써요.
explain_en: It is the 'larger' counterpart of '깜박거리다', giving a big, slow blinking feel. It describes eyes opening and closing, and also lights flickering on the verge of going out.

examples.ko: 할머니가 졸린 눈을 껌벅대며 앉아 계세요.
examples.en: Grandmother is sitting there blinking her sleepy eyes.
The cat is slowly blinking its eyes.
The puppy looked at me, blinking.

examples.ko: 눈을 자꾸 껌벅대는 걸 보니 졸린가 봐요.
examples.en: Seeing you blink so much, you must be sleepy.
The signal was flashing, so I crossed in a hurry.
Instead of answering, he just blinked.

explain: '껌벅거리다'와 거의 같은 말로, 눈이나 불빛이 느릿하게 계속 깜빡일 때 써요. 졸리거나 어리둥절해서 눈만 껌벅대는 모습을 말할 때 자주 어울려요.
explain_en: It is almost the same as '껌벅거리다' and is used for eyes or lights blinking slowly and repeatedly. It suits someone blinking blankly when sleepy or puzzled.

examples.en: Mother blinked silently.
The child is sleepy and blinking.
He blinked as if to say he understood.
Blinking, I looked around the unfamiliar room.
The streetlight was flickering, so it was a little scary.
The cow is slowly blinking its eyes.

explain: '눈을 껌벅이다'처럼 '눈을'과 함께 자주 써요. '깜박이다'의 큰말이라서 느리고 크게 깜빡이는 느낌이 있어요. 윗사람에게는 '껌벅이셨어요'처럼 높여요.
explain_en: It often pairs with '눈을', as in '눈을 껌벅이다'. As the larger counterpart of '깜박이다', it feels like slow, big blinking. For an elder, use the honorific, like '껌벅이셨어요'.

examples.en: The puppy is so happy that it bounces around.
The kids play in the snow, leaping about.
A rabbit hopped across the meadow.
I was so excited that I bounded around and fell.

examples.ko: 왜 그렇게 껑충거려요? 무슨 좋은 일 있어요?
examples.en: Why are you bouncing like that? Did something good happen?

examples.ko: 그 사람은 다리가 길어서 껑충거리며 걸어요.
examples.en: He has long legs and walks with long bouncing strides.

explain: '껑충 뛰다'가 한 번 뛰는 것이라면, '껑충거리다'는 긴 다리로 계속 뛰어오르거나 큰 걸음으로 걷는 모습이에요. 작고 가벼운 동물에는 '깡충거리다'를 쓰기도 해요.
explain_en: '껑충 뛰다' is a single leap, while '껑충거리다' means leaping repeatedly or walking with long bouncing strides. For small, light animals, '깡충거리다' is also used.

examples.en: That matter still nags at me.
Being alone in a dark room makes me uneasy.
I felt uneasy, so I checked again.

examples.ko: 꿈이 너무 이상해서 하루 종일 께름칙했어요.
examples.en: The dream was so strange that I felt uneasy all day.

examples.ko: 그 사람과 거래하는 게 왠지 께름칙해요.
examples.en: Somehow I feel uneasy about dealing with that person.
If you feel uneasy about it, it's better not to buy it.

explain: '꺼림칙하다'와 거의 같은 말이고, 마음에 걸려서 찜찜할 때 써요. 일상 대화에서는 '찜찜하다'라고도 많이 말해요.
explain_en: It is nearly the same as '꺼림칙하다', used when something nags at you and leaves you uneasy. In daily conversation people also often say '찜찜하다'.

examples.en: A crumpled, folded piece of paper came out of my pocket.

examples.ko: 꼬깃꼬깃 구겨진 만 원짜리를 펴서 냈어요.
examples.en: I smoothed out the crumpled 10,000-won bill and paid.

examples.ko: 가방 속에서 옷이 꼬깃꼬깃 다 구겨졌어요.
examples.en: The clothes got all wrinkled inside the bag.

examples.ko: 할머니가 꼬깃꼬깃 접은 돈을 손에 쥐여 주셨어요.
examples.en: Grandmother pressed some crumpled, folded money into my hand.

examples.ko: 영수증이 꼬깃꼬깃 구겨져 있어서 읽기 힘들어요.
examples.en: The receipt is so crumpled that it's hard to read.
I folded the letter up small and put it in my pocket.

explain: 종이나 천이 여러 번 접히거나 구겨져서 주름이 많은 모습이에요. '구겨지다', '접다'와 함께 자주 쓰고, '구깃구깃'과 비슷해요.
explain_en: It describes paper or cloth folded or crumpled many times and full of wrinkles. It often goes with '구겨지다' and '접다', and is similar to '구깃구깃'.

examples.en: The hen clucked.
Every morning I wake up to the cackling of hens.

examples.ko: 알을 낳은 암탉이 꼬꼬댁 하며 돌아다녀요.
examples.en: The hen that laid an egg walks around clucking.
I can hear clucking from the yard.

examples.ko: 아이가 닭을 흉내 내며 꼬꼬댁 했어요.
examples.en: The child imitated a chicken, going cluck.

examples.ko: 닭장 안에서 꼬꼬댁 소리가 크게 났어요.
examples.en: A loud cackle came from inside the henhouse.

explain: 암탉이 우는 소리를 흉내 낸 말이에요. 수탉이 아침에 우는 소리는 '꼬끼오'라고 해서 서로 달라요. 그림책이나 동화에서 자주 보여요.
explain_en: It imitates the sound a hen makes. A rooster's morning crow is '꼬끼오', so the two sounds differ. You often see it in picture books and children's stories.

examples.en: I tripped on a stone and pitched forward.
I fell flat while running and hurt my knee.

examples.ko: 그 회사가 갑자기 꼬꾸라질 줄 몰랐어요.
examples.en: I didn't know that company would suddenly collapse.
I dozed off and almost fell face-first onto the desk.
The bicycle tipped over forward and the load spilled out.
The tree was toppled by the wind.

explain: '넘어지다'보다 앞으로 거꾸러지듯 쓰러지는 느낌이 강해요. '고꾸라지다'와 같은 말이에요. 사람이 넘어질 때뿐 아니라 회사나 주가가 갑자기 무너질 때도 비유로 써요.
explain_en: Compared with '넘어지다', it strongly suggests pitching forward headfirst. It means the same as '고꾸라지다'. Besides people falling, it is also used figuratively when a company or stock price suddenly collapses.
